intro: Every day your body defends you, and every day you make choices that help it. When you scrape a knee, an army of cells rushes to clean and repair it. When a cold virus gets in, your body learns its name tag and remembers it. At the same time, you decide what to eat, when to sleep, and what to say when someone offers you something risky.

This unit has two parts. First, you will explore the immune system: the skin and mucus that block germs, the cells that eat invaders, the antibodies and memory cells that learn, and how vaccines and whole communities stay protected. Second, you will look at choices that help a growing body and brain, from food, sleep and exercise to handling peer pressure, stress and hard moments.

By the end, you will be able to explain how your body fights germs and how scientists found this out. You will be able to use facts, not fear, to think about vaping, alcohol and other drugs. You will practice refusal skills and calming skills. And you will know who to ask for help, including the 988 Lifeline.
bigQuestion: How does your body protect you, and how can your choices help it?

title: Your Body's Defenses and Choices

chapters.title: The Immune System
chapters.bigQuestion: How does your body tell friend from invader, and how can we help it do that job?

story.title: The Knee That Turned Red
story.kicker: Maya scrapes her knee at recess, and by dinner it has a story to tell.
paragraphs: Maya was racing to first base when her foot slid on the gravel. She landed hard. When she looked down, her knee was scraped raw, with little specks of dirt pressed into the skin. It stung. The school nurse rinsed it with clean water, patted it dry and covered it with a bandage.

By dinner, Maya peeled back the bandage to look. The skin around the scrape was pink and puffy. It felt warm when she touched it, warmer than her other knee. A clear, sticky fluid had dried at the edges. "Is it getting worse?" she asked her dad. He looked closely. "I think your body is busy," he said.

The next day in science class, Maya asked her teacher, Mr. Okafor, about it. He drew a circle on the board for the scrape. Then he drew tiny arrows rushing toward it. "Redness, warmth and swelling are signs of your defenders arriving," he said. "Blood vessels open wider. Cells come to eat germs and clean up. It is a busy repair site."

He added one more thing. If the redness spreads far, if it gets very painful, if pus appears or a fever starts, tell a trusted adult and see a nurse or doctor. "Most of the time your body handles a scrape well," he said. "Knowing the signs helps you know when it needs a hand." Maya looked at her knee differently after that.
story.think: What did Maya see, feel and notice about her knee, and what did each sign tell her about what her body was doing?

lessons.title: Skin and Mucus
lessons.mainIdea: Skin and mucus are barriers that keep most germs out of the body before they can cause harm.
reading: Think about the doorknob in a school hallway. Hundreds of hands touch it each day, and it carries many germs. Yet most students do not get sick from touching it. The main reason is your *skin*. Its outer layer is made of tough, flat, dead cells packed tightly together. Most germs cannot get through this wall. The skin is also slightly acidic and a little dry, which many germs do not like.

Germs can also enter through openings, such as your nose, mouth and eyes. These places are lined with *mucus*, a slippery, sticky fluid. Mucus traps dust and germs the way flypaper traps flies. In your airways, tiny hairlike parts called cilia sweep the mucus up and out. You then swallow it or cough it out. Tears and saliva also hold substances that break down some bacteria.

These barriers explain simple habits. Washing hands with soap removes germs before they reach your eyes, nose or mouth. Covering a cut with a clean bandage protects a break in the wall. Maya's scrape was a break in her skin wall. That is why the nurse cleaned it first. Barriers are the body's first line of defense, and they work all day without you noticing.

words.d: the body's outer covering, which forms a tough wall that keeps most germs out
a slippery, sticky fluid that lines the nose, throat and airways and traps germs and dust
something that blocks the way; in the body, a wall that keeps germs out

look.title: A Break in the Wall
look.text: Picture two students. One has a small paper cut on a finger and touches a dirty desk. The other has no cut and touches the same desk. Both later wash their hands with soap. The student with the cut also puts on a clean bandage.
look.prompt: Which barrier matters most for each student, and why did the bandage help?

choices: Its outer layer is made of tough cells packed tightly together
It is full of white blood cells at the surface
It makes antibodies all the time

check.why: The reading says skin's outer layer is tough, flat cells packed tightly, forming a wall most germs cannot cross.

choices: Because the scrape was a break in the skin wall
check.why: A scrape breaks the skin barrier, so cleaning removes germs before they get in.

lessons.title: Cells That Eat Germs
lessons.mainIdea: Innate immune cells respond fast to any invader, often by swallowing and destroying germs.
reading: When a germ gets past the skin, the body does not wait. Within minutes, certain white blood cells arrive. This fast, general response is called *innate immunity*. Innate means "you are born with it." These defenders do not need to have met the germ before. They react to signs that something is foreign or that tissue is damaged.

Some of these defenders are *phagocytes*, a word that means "eating cells." A phagocyte wraps itself around a germ and pulls it inside. Then it breaks the germ apart with chemicals. Neutrophils are the most common kind in the blood and are often first on the scene. Larger cells called macrophages also eat germs and clean up dead cells and debris.

In Maya's knee, phagocytes moved out of tiny blood vessels and into the scrape. They swallowed bacteria that came in with the dirt. The clear fluid she saw was partly fluid from the blood that carried these helpers. Innate defenses are quick, but they are not specially aimed. For a germ they cannot clear, the body calls in a slower, targeted team.

words.d: the body's fast, general defense that you are born with and that reacts to any invader
a white blood cell that swallows and destroys germs and debris; the name means eating cell
a blood cell that helps defend the body against germs

look.cite: MedlinePlus, U.S. National Library of Medicine, "Blood Differential Test," typical adult ranges, rounded
look.prompt: Which kind of white blood cell is most common, and why might it make sense for first responders to be plentiful?

check.q: What does innate mean in innate immunity?
check.why: Innate means you are born with it; this defense does not need to have met the germ before.

check.q: How does a phagocyte destroy a germ?
choices: It wraps around the germ, pulls it inside and breaks it apart
It blocks the nose with mucus
It sends the germ to the stomach
check.why: Phagocyte means eating cell; it swallows the germ and breaks it down with chemicals.

check.q: According to the data, which white blood cells are most common?
check.why: Neutrophils make up about 60 percent of white cells, the largest share in the table.

lessons.title: Inflammation: Red, Warm, Swollen
lessons.mainIdea: Inflammation brings blood, fluid and defender cells to an injured or infected place, which causes redness, warmth and swelling.
reading: Maya's knee turned red, warm and puffy. These are the signs of *inflammation*. Doctors in ancient Rome described four signs of it: redness, heat, swelling and pain. The Roman writer Celsus listed them about 2,000 years ago. Doctors still use the same list today. Later, a fifth sign was added: the injured part may not work as well for a while.

Here is what causes each sign. Damaged cells and defender cells release chemical signals. The signals tell nearby blood vessels to widen. More blood flows in, which makes the skin red and warm. The vessel walls also become leakier. Fluid and white blood cells slip out into the tissue, which causes swelling. Some signals press on nerve endings, which causes pain.

Inflammation is a helpful part of healing. It brings defenders and repair materials to the right spot. It usually calms down in a few days as the area heals. But inflammation that spreads, grows worse or comes with fever can be a sign of infection. That is the time to tell a trusted adult and see a nurse or doctor. They can decide whether more care is needed.

words.d: the body's response to injury or infection, bringing blood and defender cells and causing redness, warmth, swelling and pain
a tube, such as a capillary or vein, that carries blood through the body

look.title: An Ancient List
look.text: The signs of inflammation are four: redness and swelling, with heat and pain.
look.cite: Aulus Cornelius Celsus, De Medicina, c. 30 CE (paraphrase of a Latin passage)
look.prompt: Which of Celsus's four signs did Maya notice, and what causes each one?

check.q: Why does an inflamed area look red and feel warm?
choices: Mucus builds up on the skin
Blood vessels widen and more blood flows in
check.why: Chemical signals widen blood vessels, bringing more warm blood to the area.

check.q: What causes the swelling in inflammation?
choices: Fluid and white cells leaking out of leaky vessels
check.why: Vessel walls become leakier, and fluid and white cells move into the tissue, causing swelling.

check.q: When should inflammation lead you to tell an adult and see a nurse or doctor?
choices: When it spreads, grows worse or comes with fever
Only if it lasts a year
Never, because inflammation is always helpful
check.why: The reading says spreading, worsening or fever can signal infection that needs care.

lessons.title: B Cells and T Cells
lessons.mainIdea: Lymphocytes called B cells and T cells learn to recognize one specific germ and attack it.
reading: Suppose a cold virus gets into your nose and throat. The innate defenders fight it, but the virus keeps making copies. After several days, a second team takes over. This is *adaptive immunity*, the part of the immune system that learns. It is slower to start, but it aims at one exact germ. That is often why a cold is worst for a few days and then gets better.

The adaptive team is made of *lymphocytes*, a kind of white blood cell. There are two main kinds. B cells make antibodies, which you will study next. T cells do other jobs. Helper T cells send signals that direct the whole response. Killer T cells find body cells that a virus has taken over and destroy them, so the virus cannot keep copying itself.

How do these cells know what to attack? Each germ carries molecules on its surface called *antigens*. An antigen is like a name tag. Each B or T cell recognizes one shape of name tag. When a cell finds its match, it multiplies into an army of copies, all aimed at that germ. Lymph nodes, the small lumps in your neck, are where many of these meetings happen. That is why they can swell when you are sick.

words.d: the part of the immune system that learns to recognize and target one specific germ
a white blood cell, such as a B cell or T cell, that carries out adaptive immunity
a molecule, often on a germ's surface, that the immune system recognizes like a name tag

look.title: Swollen Glands
look.text: Jordan has a sore throat. His mom gently feels the sides of his neck and finds two small, tender lumps. "Your lymph nodes are working," she says. A few days later his throat feels better, and the lumps shrink.
look.prompt: Using the words lymphocyte and antigen, explain what was happening in Jordan's lymph nodes.

check.q: What makes adaptive immunity different from innate immunity?
choices: It only works in the skin
It learns and aims at one specific germ
check.why: Adaptive immunity is slower to start but targets one exact germ.

check.q: What do killer T cells do?
choices: Destroy body cells a virus has taken over
check.why: Killer T cells find infected body cells and destroy them so the virus cannot keep copying.

check.q: An antigen is best described as what?
choices: A molecule on a germ that works like a name tag
check.why: Antigens are surface molecules the immune system recognizes, like a name tag.

lessons.title: Antibodies
lessons.mainIdea: Antibodies are Y-shaped proteins made by B cells that lock onto one antigen and mark or block a germ.
reading: When a B cell finds its matching antigen, it multiplies. Many of the new cells become antibody factories. An *antibody* is a Y-shaped protein. The tips of the Y fit one antigen, like a key fits one lock. One of these factory cells can release thousands of antibodies every second into the blood.

Antibodies help in several ways. They can coat a virus so it cannot enter your cells. This is called neutralizing it. They can clump germs together so they are easier to catch. They also act like flags. A germ covered in antibodies is much easier for phagocytes to find and eat. In this way, the adaptive and innate teams work together.

Doctors can test the blood for antibodies. Finding antibodies to a certain germ shows the body has met it, through an infection or a vaccine. For example, before some jobs in hospitals, workers may have a blood test to check for antibodies to measles. That test tells the doctor whether the person is likely protected.

words.d: a Y-shaped protein made by B cells that locks onto one specific antigen
to block a germ, such as by coating a virus so it cannot enter cells

look.title: Lock and Key
look.text: Imagine a hallway of lockers. Each locker has a different lock shape. You hold a ring of keys, and each key fits only one lock. An antibody is like one of those keys. It fits one antigen shape and no other.
look.prompt: How does this picture explain why an antibody to measles does not protect you from chickenpox?

check.q: Which cells make antibodies?
check.why: B cells that meet their matching antigen multiply, and many become antibody factories.

check.q: How do antibodies help phagocytes?
choices: They flag germs so phagocytes can find and eat them
check.why: Antibodies coat germs and act like flags that help phagocytes find them.

check.q: What does a blood test that finds measles antibodies show?
choices: The person has a cold now
The person has never met measles
The body has met measles through infection or a vaccine
check.why: Antibodies to a germ show the body has met it before, by infection or vaccine.

lessons.title: Memory Cells
lessons.mainIdea: After an infection, memory cells stay in the body and let it respond faster and stronger the next time.
reading: Many people who had chickenpox as children never get it again. Why? After the fight is over, most of the extra B and T cells die off. But some stay behind for years, sometimes for life. These are *memory cells*. They remember the antigen of the germ they fought.

The first time you meet a germ, the adaptive response can take a week or more to build up. That is the *primary response*. If the same germ returns, memory cells spring into action at once. They multiply fast and make large amounts of antibodies within days. This faster second round is called the secondary response. Often it stops the germ before you ever feel sick.

Memory has limits. Some germs change their name tags. Flu viruses change a little each year, so old memory cells may not fully match. That is one reason a new flu shot is offered each year. Other germs, like measles, change very little. So protection against measles can last a very long time.

words.d: a long-lived B or T cell that remembers a germ and helps the body respond fast if it returns
the body's first, slower adaptive response to a germ it has never met

look.title: First Time, Second Time
look.text: Picture two graphs of antibody levels. In the first, after a germ arrives, the line stays low for about a week, then rises slowly to a small hill. In the second, when the same germ returns months later, the line shoots up within a few days to a tall mountain.
look.prompt: Which graph shows the primary response, which shows the secondary response, and what makes the difference?

check.q: What do memory cells remember?
choices: The antigen of a germ they fought
The shape of your skin cells
check.why: Memory cells remember the antigen of the germ and respond fast if it returns.

check.q: Why is a new flu shot offered each year?
choices: Flu viruses change a little each year
Memory cells last only one day
check.why: Flu viruses change their surface slightly, so old memory cells may not fully match.

check.q: How is the secondary response different from the primary response?
choices: It happens only in the skin
check.why: Memory cells make the second response faster and larger, often before you feel sick.

lessons.title: How Vaccines Build Memory
lessons.mainIdea: A vaccine shows the immune system a harmless version or piece of a germ so it builds memory cells without the illness.
reading: In 1796, the English doctor Edward Jenner tested an idea he had heard among farm workers. Milkmaids who caught cowpox, a mild disease from cows, seemed not to catch smallpox, a deadly disease. Jenner took material from a cowpox sore and put it into a small cut on the arm of a boy named James Phipps. Later he exposed the boy to smallpox material, and the boy did not get sick. Today such a test on a child would not be allowed. But it launched the idea of the *vaccine*. The word comes from vacca, Latin for cow.

A vaccine works by giving the immune system a safe preview. It may hold a weakened germ, a killed germ, a piece of a germ, or instructions for cells to make one harmless germ protein. The immune system sees the antigen and builds B cells, T cells and memory cells. The person gains *immunity*, protection from the disease, without having to get sick first.

Vaccines are tested in large studies before they are approved, and they keep being watched afterward. Like any medicine, they can have side effects. Most are mild, such as a sore arm or a day of tiredness, which are signs the immune system is working. Serious reactions are rare. Your doctor or nurse can answer questions about which vaccines are recommended and why.

words.d: a preparation that safely shows the immune system a germ or part of one so it builds memory
protection from a disease because the immune system can recognize and fight it

look.title: Jenner Reports His Test
look.text: Jenner described placing matter from a cowpox sore into the arm of a boy, and later placing smallpox matter into him, and reported that the boy did not take the smallpox.
look.cite: Edward Jenner, An Inquiry into the Causes and Effects of the Variolae Vaccinae, 1798 (paraphrase)
look.prompt: What did Jenner observe, what did he test, and why would scientists today want many more people in a study?

check.q: What gave Jenner the idea for his test?
choices: Milkmaids with cowpox seemed not to catch smallpox
A microscope photo of a virus
check.why: Jenner tested a farm observation that milkmaids who had cowpox seemed not to catch smallpox.

check.q: How does a vaccine lead to immunity?
choices: It kills every germ in the body
It shows the immune system an antigen so it builds memory cells
check.why: A vaccine safely presents an antigen, and the body builds B, T and memory cells.

check.q: What does a sore arm after a vaccine usually mean?
choices: The person now has the disease
The person needs a second arm
check.why: The reading says mild side effects like a sore arm are signs the immune system is working.

lessons.title: Herd Immunity
lessons.mainIdea: When enough people in a community are immune, a germ has trouble spreading, which also protects people who cannot be vaccinated.
reading: Picture a baby too young for the measles vaccine, and a classmate being treated for cancer whose immune system is weak. Neither can be fully protected by vaccines. Yet they can still be shielded. If nearly everyone around them is immune, the measles virus has almost no one to jump to. It dies out before it reaches them.

This shielding is called *herd immunity*, or community immunity. It works because a germ spreads from person to person. Each immune person is like a missing link in the chain. The more links are missing, the harder it is for the germ to travel. The share of people who must be immune depends on how contagious a germ is. A *contagious* disease is one that spreads easily between people.

Measles is one of the most contagious diseases known. Experts estimate that about 95 of every 100 people need to be immune to stop its spread. Diseases that spread less easily need a lower share. When vaccination rates in a community drop, outbreaks can return. That happened with measles in several U.S. communities in recent years. Public health workers track these rates to keep communities safe.

words.d: protection for a whole community when enough people are immune that a germ cannot spread easily
able to spread easily from one person to another

look.title: How Many Need to Be Immune?
look.cite: Paul Fine, "Herd Immunity: History, Theory, Practice," Epidemiologic Reviews, 1993; rounded estimates
look.prompt: Which disease needs the highest share immune, and what does that tell you about how contagious it is?

check.q: Who does herd immunity help protect?
choices: Only people who are already sick
People who cannot be vaccinated, like young babies
check.why: When most people are immune, the germ cannot reach those who cannot be vaccinated.

check.q: Why does measles need a very high share of people to be immune?
check.why: Measles is one of the most contagious diseases, so about 95 percent must be immune.

check.q: In the chain picture, what is an immune person like?
choices: A missing link that the germ cannot pass through
check.why: Each immune person breaks the chain of spread, like a missing link.

sections.title: When Defenses Misfire, and How We Know

lessons.title: Allergies
lessons.mainIdea: An allergy happens when the immune system overreacts to something harmless, like pollen or peanuts.
reading: Every spring, Luis gets itchy eyes and a runny nose when the trees bloom. Tree pollen is harmless to most people. But Luis's immune system treats it as an invader. An *allergy* is an immune reaction to something that is not actually dangerous. The harmless thing that sets it off is called an *allergen*.

In an allergy, the body makes a special kind of antibody against the allergen. These antibodies sit on cells that hold a chemical called histamine. When the allergen shows up again, those cells release histamine. It causes sneezing, itching, watery eyes or hives. Common allergens include pollen, dust mites, pet dander, some foods, and insect stings. A study led by Dr. Ruchi Gupta in Chicago, published in 2018, estimated that about 8 in 100 U.S. children have a food allergy.

Most allergies are an annoyance that can be managed. A doctor can help find the allergen and suggest ways to avoid it or medicines to ease the signs. A few people have a severe, whole-body reaction called anaphylaxis, which can make breathing hard. It needs emergency care right away. People with severe allergies may carry an epinephrine auto-injector and a plan made with their doctor. Friends who know the plan can help.

words.d: an immune reaction to something that is usually harmless
a harmless substance, such as pollen or peanuts, that sets off an allergy
a chemical released during an allergy that causes itching, sneezing and swelling

look.title: A Classroom Plan
look.text: A new classmate, Ana, has a severe peanut allergy. Her teacher explains that Ana carries an epinephrine auto-injector, that the class will not share snacks, and that if Ana says her throat feels tight, someone should get an adult right away.
look.prompt: How does each part of this plan help Ana, and what could you do if you were her friend?

check.q: What is an allergen?
choices: A harmless substance that sets off an allergy
check.why: An allergen is something usually harmless, like pollen, that triggers an allergy.

check.q: Which chemical causes sneezing and itching in an allergy?
check.why: Cells release histamine when the allergen returns, causing itching and sneezing.

check.q: What should happen if someone has signs of anaphylaxis?
choices: Tell them to run a lap
check.why: Anaphylaxis is a severe whole-body reaction that needs emergency care at once.

lessons.title: When the Body Targets Itself
lessons.mainIdea: In an autoimmune condition, the immune system mistakes some of the body's own cells for invaders.
reading: Normally, the immune system learns to leave the body's own cells alone. It learns this while immune cells are developing. Sometimes this learning slips. In an *autoimmune condition*, the immune system attacks some of the body's own healthy tissue. Auto means "self." Scientists are still studying why this happens. Genes and things in the environment both seem to play a part.

Here are a few examples, named simply. In type 1 diabetes, the immune system attacks the cells in the pancreas that make insulin, the hormone that lets cells use sugar. In celiac disease, eating gluten, a protein in wheat, leads the immune system to harm the lining of the small intestine. In rheumatoid arthritis, it attacks the lining of joints, causing pain and swelling.

Autoimmune conditions are not caused by anything a person did, and they are not contagious. Many people live full, active lives with them. Treatment depends on the condition. A person with type 1 diabetes takes insulin. A person with celiac disease eats gluten-free food. Doctors, nurses and dietitians help each person make a plan that fits their body.

words.d: a condition in which the immune system attacks some of the body's own healthy cells
a hormone made in the pancreas that helps the body's cells use sugar for energy

look.title: Two Kinds of Mistakes
look.text: Side by side: In an allergy, the immune system overreacts to something from outside, like pollen. In an autoimmune condition, the immune system reacts to something inside, the body's own cells. Both are cases of the defense system aiming at the wrong target.
look.prompt: How are allergies and autoimmune conditions alike, and how are they different?

check.q: What does auto mean in autoimmune?
check.why: Auto means self; in autoimmune conditions the immune system targets the body's own cells.

check.q: In type 1 diabetes, what does the immune system attack?
choices: Cells in the pancreas that make insulin
check.why: In type 1 diabetes, the immune system attacks the insulin-making cells of the pancreas.

check.q: Which statement about autoimmune conditions is true?
choices: They are caused by bad choices
They cannot be treated at all
They are not contagious, and treatment depends on the condition
check.why: The reading says they are not contagious or caused by the person, and each has its own treatment.

lessons.title: How Scientists Found Out
lessons.mainIdea: We know about immunity because scientists observed carefully, tested ideas and changed their thinking when evidence demanded it.
reading: For about 2,000 years, many European and Middle Eastern doctors followed the idea of the four humors. They thought illness came from an imbalance of four body fluids. In the 1860s and 1870s, Louis Pasteur in France and Robert Koch in Germany showed that specific germs cause specific diseases. This *germ theory* replaced the humors because experiments supported it again and again.

In 1882, the Russian scientist Élie Metchnikoff was studying see-through starfish larvae in Italy. He pushed a tiny rose thorn into one. The next day, he saw moving cells gathered around the thorn. He guessed these cells defend the body by swallowing invaders. He named them phagocytes. Around the same time, Paul Ehrlich in Germany studied substances in the blood, later called antibodies. In 1908, the two men shared the Nobel Prize for their work on immunity.

Science keeps building on earlier work. Microscopes, lab tests and large *clinical trials* have shown how B cells, T cells and memory cells work. A clinical trial is a careful study that tests a treatment in people, often comparing it to a group that does not get it. Each new finding is checked by other scientists. That is how the ideas in this chapter became trusted.

words.d: the scientific idea, supported by experiments, that many diseases are caused by specific germs
a careful study that tests a treatment or vaccine in people, often comparing groups

review.why: Skin and mucus are barriers that keep most germs out before other defenses are needed.

She was allergic to her bandage
Her skin had turned into mucus

choices: Memory cells respond fast if it returns

It makes the baby's skin thicker
Immune people around the baby stop the germ from spreading

An allergy reacts to a harmless outside substance; autoimmunity targets the body's own cells

choices: Experiments supported it again and again

chapters.title: Healthy Choices and Hard Things
chapters.bigQuestion: What helps a growing body and brain thrive, and how can you make good choices when things get hard?

story.title: The Offer at the Party
story.kicker: At a friend's birthday party, Dev is handed a vape and has about three seconds to decide.
paragraphs: The music was loud in Kayla's basement. Dev was laughing at a video with two friends when an older boy he barely knew walked over. He held out a small, bright blue device that smelled like candy. "Try it," he said. "Everybody does. It's just flavor." A few kids turned to watch.

Dev's heart beat faster. He wanted to fit in. But a picture popped into his head from health class the week before. Ms. Rivera had shown the class a list of what is often in a vape. Most contain nicotine, even some labeled as just flavor. She had explained that a teen brain is still building its connections, and nicotine can change how those connections form.

He also remembered the practice they did in pairs. Say no clearly. Give a short reason if you want. Suggest something else, or walk away. Dev took a breath. "No thanks, I'm good," he said. "Hey, Sam, want to get some pizza?" Sam nodded, and the two of them headed upstairs. Nobody made a big deal of it.

Later that night, Dev told his older sister what happened. She said she was proud of him. She also said that if he ever felt stuck at a party, he could text her a code word and she would call with a reason for him to leave. Dev saved the plan in his phone. He felt steadier knowing he had one.
story.think: Which facts and skills from health class helped Dev decide, and what made his plan work in the moment?

lessons.title: Food for a Growing Body
lessons.mainIdea: Teens grow fast, so they need a variety of foods that give energy, protein, calcium and other nutrients.
reading: Between about ages 10 and 16, many young people grow several inches in just a few years. Bones get longer and denser. Muscles grow. All that building takes *nutrients*, the substances in food the body uses for energy, growth and repair. A growing teen often needs more food than a younger child, and that is normal.

The U.S. Department of Agriculture uses a simple picture called MyPlate, introduced in 2011. It shows a plate about half filled with fruits and vegetables, about a quarter with grains, and about a quarter with protein foods, plus a serving of dairy or a calcium-rich food. Whole grains, like brown rice or whole-wheat bread, give more fiber than white bread. Calcium from milk, yogurt, fortified soy drinks or leafy greens helps build strong bones.

Healthy eating is about patterns over time, not about one perfect meal. A *balanced diet* has many kinds of food, including foods from your family's culture. Drinking water instead of sugary drinks most of the time helps too. Skipping meals can leave you tired and unfocused. If you have questions about food, allergies or your body, a doctor, school nurse or dietitian can help.

words.d: a substance in food, such as protein or calcium, that the body uses for energy, growth or repair
a pattern of eating many kinds of food in healthy amounts over time
a mineral found in foods like milk and leafy greens that helps build strong bones

look.title: Build a Plate
look.text: Tanya's lunch: a turkey and cheese sandwich on whole-wheat bread, carrot sticks, and a bottle of water. Marcus's lunch: a bag of chips, a cookie, and a large soda. Both students have a long soccer practice after school.
look.prompt: Using MyPlate, what food groups does each lunch include, and what one change would help Marcus most at practice?

check.q: What are nutrients?
choices: Substances in food the body uses for energy, growth and repair
check.why: Nutrients are the substances in food the body uses to get energy, grow and repair.

check.q: According to MyPlate, about how much of the plate should be fruits and vegetables?
check.why: MyPlate shows about half the plate as fruits and vegetables.

check.q: Which food helps build strong bones because of its calcium?
check.why: The reading lists milk, yogurt, fortified soy drinks and leafy greens as calcium sources.

lessons.title: Sleep: The Brain's Night Shift
lessons.mainIdea: Teens need about 8 to 10 hours of sleep a night, because sleep helps the brain learn and the body grow and heal.
reading: Jalen stayed up past midnight on his phone. At 6:30 the next morning, his alarm rang. In math class, he could not focus, and he snapped at a friend. Many students know this feeling. Sleep is not wasted time. While you sleep, your brain sorts and stores what you learned that day. Your body releases growth hormone and repairs muscles.

Sleep experts at the American Academy of Sleep Medicine recommend 8 to 10 hours a night for teens ages 13 to 18, and 9 to 12 hours for children ages 6 to 12. In puberty, the body clock also shifts. Teens often feel sleepy later at night than younger children do. This shift is a normal part of growing up, called a change in *circadian rhythm*, the body's daily clock.

Good *sleep habits* can help. Go to bed and wake up at about the same time each day, even on weekends. Put screens away about an hour before bed, since bright light can signal the brain to stay awake. Keep the room dark and cool. Caffeine from soda, coffee or energy drinks can make sleep harder. If you often cannot sleep, talk to a parent or doctor.

words.d: the body's roughly 24-hour internal clock that controls when you feel sleepy and awake
daily routines, like a regular bedtime and no screens before bed, that help you sleep well

look.title: How Much Sleep?
look.cite: American Academy of Sleep Medicine, consensus statement on sleep for children and teens, 2016
look.prompt: How many hours does a 14-year-old need, and how does that compare with Jalen's night?

check.q: How many hours of sleep do sleep experts recommend for teens ages 13 to 18?
check.why: The American Academy of Sleep Medicine recommends 8 to 10 hours for teens.

check.q: What does the brain do during sleep?
choices: Sorts and stores what you learned
check.why: While you sleep, the brain sorts and stores the day's learning.

check.q: Which habit helps sleep?
choices: Drinking an energy drink at night
Putting screens away about an hour before bed
check.why: Bright screen light can keep the brain awake, so putting screens away helps.

lessons.title: Moving Your Body
lessons.mainIdea: Young people are advised to get about 60 minutes of physical activity each day, which helps the heart, bones, mood and sleep.
reading: Physical activity does not have to mean a team sport. Walking the dog, dancing in your room, biking to a friend's house and playing tag all count. The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, in its Physical Activity Guidelines of 2018, advises children and teens ages 6 to 17 to get 60 minutes or more of activity every day.

Most of that time should be *aerobic activity*, movement that makes your heart beat faster and your breathing quicker, like running, swimming or dancing. On at least three days a week, the guidelines also include muscle-strengthening activity, like climbing or push-ups, and bone-strengthening activity, like jumping. Bones grow stronger when they carry weight and land from jumps.

Activity helps more than muscles. It strengthens the heart and lungs. Many studies link it to better mood, lower stress and better sleep. Every body can move in its own way. A student who uses a wheelchair might play wheelchair basketball or do seated strength work. A physical therapist, coach or doctor can help anyone find activities that fit their body and that they enjoy.

words.d: any movement of the body that uses energy, like walking, dancing or playing sports
movement that makes your heart beat faster and your breathing quicker for a while

look.title: The Daily Goal
look.text: Children and adolescents ages 6 through 17 should do 60 minutes or more of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity daily, including muscle- and bone-strengthening activity on at least 3 days a week.
look.cite: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans, 2nd edition, 2018 (paraphrase)
look.prompt: List three ways you could reach 60 minutes in one day without joining a team.

check.q: How much daily activity do the guidelines advise for ages 6 to 17?
check.why: The 2018 Physical Activity Guidelines advise 60 minutes or more every day.

check.q: Which is an example of aerobic activity?
choices: Dancing that makes your heart beat faster
check.why: Aerobic activity raises your heart rate and breathing, like dancing or running.

check.q: What helps bones grow stronger?
choices: Carrying weight and landing from jumps
check.why: The reading says bones get stronger when they carry weight and land from jumps.

lessons.title: A Brain Under Construction
lessons.mainIdea: The teen brain is still developing, especially the prefrontal cortex, which helps with planning and self-control.
reading: Your brain is about as big as an adult's by around age 11 or 12. But it keeps changing inside for years. Brain scans show that pathways used often get stronger and faster, while ones rarely used get trimmed away. This makes the teen years a powerful time for learning new skills.

Different parts finish at different times. The *prefrontal cortex*, the area just behind your forehead, helps you plan, weigh choices and control impulses. Research suggests it keeps developing into the mid-20s. Areas linked to emotions and rewards become very active in the teen years. That can make excitement and friends feel especially important. This is a normal stage, not a flaw.

Because the brain is still wiring itself, what it is exposed to matters. Learning, sleep and exercise help build strong pathways. *Addiction* is a condition in which a person keeps using a substance even when it causes harm, because the brain has come to crave it. Scientists have found that the younger a person starts using nicotine, alcohol or other drugs, the higher the chance of addiction later.

words.d: the part of the brain behind the forehead that helps with planning, choices and self-control
a condition in which a person keeps using a substance or doing something even when it causes harm

look.title: Paths in the Grass
look.text: Picture a grassy field between two school buildings. Where students walk every day, a clear dirt path forms. Where no one walks, grass grows back over the old trail. Brain pathways work a bit like this: the ones you use often get stronger.
look.prompt: What is one healthy skill you could practice so its brain pathway gets stronger?

check.q: What does the prefrontal cortex help with?
check.why: The prefrontal cortex, behind the forehead, helps with planning and impulse control.

check.q: About when does research suggest the prefrontal cortex finishes developing?
check.why: The reading says it keeps developing into the mid-20s.

check.q: What have scientists found about starting substance use young?
choices: It raises the chance of addiction later
check.why: The younger a person starts, the higher the chance of addiction later.

lessons.title: Vaping and Nicotine
lessons.mainIdea: Most vapes contain nicotine, which is addictive and can affect the developing teen brain.
reading: A *vape*, or e-cigarette, is a battery-powered device that heats a liquid into an aerosol that a person breathes in. The liquid often has flavors like fruit or candy. Many young people think vapes are just flavored water. But most vapes sold in the United States contain *nicotine*, the same addictive drug found in tobacco. Some labeled nicotine-free have been found to contain it.

In 2016, the U.S. Surgeon General issued a report on e-cigarettes and young people. It explained that nicotine exposure during the teen years can harm the developing brain. It can affect attention, learning and mood, and it makes addiction more likely. Some vapes deliver a lot of nicotine, so a person can become dependent quickly. Dependent means the body feels uncomfortable without it.

The aerosol is not just harmless water vapor. It can contain tiny particles and chemicals that are breathed deep into the lungs. The good news is that most teens do not vape. In a 2023 national survey, about 90 in 100 high school students said they had not vaped in the past month. People who want to quit can get free help from a doctor, a school counselor, or programs like the text line This Is Quitting.

words.d: an e-cigarette; a battery-powered device that heats a liquid into an aerosol to breathe in
an addictive drug found in tobacco and in most vapes
a mist of tiny particles or droplets in the air

look.title: Students Who Vaped in the Past Month
look.cite: CDC and FDA, National Youth Tobacco Survey, 2023
look.prompt: What share of high school students did not vape in the past month? What does that tell you about the idea that everybody does it?

check.q: What addictive drug is in most vapes?
check.why: Most vapes contain nicotine, the same addictive drug found in tobacco.

check.q: What did the 2016 Surgeon General report explain?
choices: Nicotine in the teen years can harm the developing brain
check.why: The report said nicotine exposure in adolescence can harm the developing brain.

check.q: What does the 2023 survey data show?
choices: Middle schoolers vape more than high schoolers
check.why: About 10 percent of high schoolers vaped in the past month, so about 90 percent did not.

lessons.title: Alcohol and Other Drugs
lessons.mainIdea: Alcohol and other drugs change how the brain works, and they carry extra risks for a brain that is still developing.
reading: Alcohol is a *depressant*, a drug that slows down the brain and body. Even small amounts can slow reaction time and affect judgment and balance. That is one reason it is illegal to drive after drinking, and why it is illegal to buy alcohol in the United States before age 21. Larger amounts can make breathing slow down, which is a medical emergency.

Other drugs affect the brain in different ways. Cannabis, also called marijuana, can affect memory, attention and coordination. It is legal for adults 21 and older in Illinois since 2020, but not for teens. Some of today's cannabis products are much stronger than in the past. Prescription medicines are safe when used as a doctor directs. Taking someone else's pills, or taking more than directed, can be dangerous.

One serious risk today is fake pills. Some pills sold outside pharmacies look like real medicine but contain fentanyl, a very strong opioid. A tiny amount can stop a person's breathing. Only take medicine from a pharmacist or trusted adult. If someone seems very sleepy, will not wake up or is breathing strangely, call 911 right away. Illinois has a law that protects people who call for help in an overdose.

words.d: a drug, such as alcohol, that slows down the brain and body
a strong kind of drug, including some pain medicines and fentanyl, that can slow or stop breathing
taking so much of a drug that it seriously harms the body

look.title: What Would You Do?
look.text: At a sleepover, a friend shows you a pill he says will help you feel relaxed. He got it from someone online. It looks just like a pill from a pharmacy, with letters stamped on it.
look.prompt: Using facts from the reading, explain why this pill is risky and what you could say and do.

check.q: What is a depressant?
choices: A drug that speeds up the brain
A drug that slows the brain and body
check.why: Alcohol is a depressant; it slows down the brain and body.

check.q: Why are pills bought outside a pharmacy risky?
choices: They may contain fentanyl even if they look real
They are too big to swallow
check.why: Fake pills can look real but contain fentanyl, which can stop breathing.

check.q: What should you do if someone will not wake up or is breathing strangely?
check.why: These are signs of an emergency, and the reading says to call 911 right away.

lessons.title: Understanding Peer Pressure
lessons.mainIdea: Peer pressure is the pull to do what others your age do, and it can push toward good or risky choices.
reading: When Aisha's friends joined the robotics club, she joined too, and she found she loved building. When Omar's friends started skipping lunch to look thinner, he felt pushed to skip it too. Both are examples of *peer pressure*, the influence that people your own age have on what you do. Peers are people in your age group, like classmates and friends.

Peer pressure can be spoken, like "Come on, just try it." It can also be unspoken. Nobody says a word, but you notice what everyone is wearing or doing and feel you should match. People often overestimate how many peers are doing a risky thing. Survey data, like the vaping numbers you just read, often show that far fewer are doing it than it seems.

Wanting to belong is a normal and healthy human need. The key is noticing the pull and asking yourself a few questions. Is this safe? Does it match who I want to be? Would I be okay if my family knew? Choosing friends who respect your choices makes hard moments easier. Positive peer pressure, like friends who study together or cheer each other on, can help you grow.

words.d: the influence that people your own age have on what you think and do
a person in your own age group, like a classmate or friend

look.title: Spoken or Unspoken?
look.text: Scene 1: A classmate says, "If you don't cheat on this quiz with us, you're boring." Scene 2: At lunch, everyone at your table has the same expensive shoes. Nobody says anything, but you start asking your parents for a pair.
look.prompt: Which scene shows spoken pressure and which shows unspoken pressure? How might you respond to each?

check.q: Which is an example of positive peer pressure?
choices: Friends pushing you to skip lunch
Friends inviting you to join the robotics club
check.why: Aisha's friends led her to a club she loved, which is a positive influence.

check.q: What is unspoken peer pressure?
choices: Feeling you should match what others do without anyone asking
check.why: Unspoken pressure comes from noticing what others do and feeling you should match.

check.q: What do surveys often show about risky behavior among peers?
choices: Fewer people are doing it than it seems
check.why: People often overestimate how many peers are doing a risky thing.

lessons.title: Refusal Skills
lessons.mainIdea: Refusal skills are clear, practiced ways to say no while staying calm and keeping your friendships.
reading: Remember Dev at the party. He did not give a speech. He said, "No thanks, I'm good," and suggested pizza. These are *refusal skills*, ways to say no that you plan and practice ahead of time. Practicing helps because in a stressful moment, the brain reaches for what it already knows.

Here are steps many health teachers use. Say no clearly and early, and use a firm voice. Give a short reason if you want: "I have a game tomorrow." Suggest something else to do. If the pressure keeps going, leave. Body language matters too. Stand tall, look at the person, and keep your voice steady. You do not need to explain or argue.

A backup plan helps. Some families use a code word, like Dev's sister. A teen texts it, and the adult calls with a reason to leave, no questions asked in the moment. A true friend will respect your no. If someone keeps pushing or makes fun of you, that tells you something about the situation. Walking away is a strong choice, not a weak one.

words.d: clear, practiced ways to say no to something you do not want to do
messages you send with your posture, face and voice, without words

look.title: Practice Script
look.text: Friend: "Let's take the shortcut across the train tracks." You: "No, I'm not doing that." Friend: "Why not? It's faster." You: "It's not safe. Let's take the bridge and grab a snack on the way." Friend: "Fine, whatever."
look.prompt: Find each refusal step in the script: saying no, giving a reason, and suggesting something else.

check.q: Why does practicing refusal skills ahead of time help?
choices: In a stressful moment, the brain reaches for what it already knows
check.why: The reading says practice helps because the brain uses what it already knows under stress.

check.q: Which is a refusal step from the reading?
choices: Argue until the other person agrees
check.why: Suggesting another activity is one of the listed refusal steps.

check.q: What does a code word plan let a teen do?
choices: Text an adult who calls with a reason to leave
check.why: A code word lets a teen signal an adult, who calls with a reason to leave.

lessons.title: Stress and Anxiety
lessons.mainIdea: Stress is the body's response to a challenge, and there are skills that help calm it and ways to get help when it feels too big.
reading: The night before a big test, Priya's stomach felt tight and her heart beat fast. That is *stress*, the body's response to a challenge or demand. When the brain senses a challenge, it releases hormones like adrenaline and cortisol. They speed up the heart and breathing and give a burst of energy. In small doses, stress can help you focus and rise to the moment.

*Anxiety* is a feeling of worry or unease about what might happen. Everyone feels it sometimes. When worry is strong, lasts a long time, or gets in the way of school, sleep or friends, it is worth talking to a doctor or counselor. Anxiety is very common and very treatable. Counseling and other care help many people feel better.

Some *coping skills* help calm the body. Slow breathing, like breathing in for four counts and out for six, can slow a racing heart. Moving your body, getting enough sleep, spending time outside, and talking with someone you trust all help. Breaking a big task into small steps can make it feel possible. Different skills work for different people, so it helps to try a few and notice what works for you.

words.d: the body's response to a challenge or demand, often with a faster heartbeat and breathing
a feeling of worry or unease about what might happen
a healthy action, like slow breathing or talking to someone, that helps you handle stress

look.title: Try It: Slow Breathing
look.text: Sit comfortably. Put one hand on your belly. Breathe in slowly through your nose while you count to four. Feel your belly rise. Then breathe out slowly through your mouth while you count to six. Repeat five times. Notice how your shoulders and heartbeat feel afterward.
look.prompt: What did you notice in your body? When during a school day could this skill help you?

check.q: Which hormones does the body release during stress?
check.why: The reading names adrenaline and cortisol as stress hormones.

check.q: When is anxiety worth talking to a doctor or counselor about?
choices: Only if you feel it once
When it is strong, lasts long or gets in the way of daily life
check.why: Strong, lasting anxiety that interferes with school, sleep or friends is worth getting help for.

check.q: Which is a coping skill from the reading?
choices: Breathing in for four counts and out for six
Staying up all night to worry
check.why: Slow breathing is a coping skill that can slow a racing heart.

lessons.title: Asking for Help
lessons.mainIdea: Asking for help is a strength, and trusted adults, counselors and the 988 Lifeline are there when things feel too heavy.
reading: Sometimes feelings get too heavy to carry alone. A student might feel sad for weeks, lose interest in things they used to enjoy, or have thoughts of hurting themselves. These are signs to reach out right away. Asking for help is a sign of strength and good sense, just like going to a doctor for a broken arm.

Who can help? A *trusted adult* is a grown-up who listens and helps keep you safe, like a parent, relative, teacher, coach, school nurse or school counselor. You can say something simple: "I've been feeling really down, and I need to talk." If a friend tells you they are thinking about hurting themselves, do not keep it a secret. Tell a trusted adult right away. That is what a good friend does.

Help is also available any time, day or night. In July 2022, the United States launched *988*, the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline. Anyone can call or text 988, or chat online, for free. Trained counselors listen and help people who are in emotional distress or worried about someone else. If someone is in immediate danger, call 911.

words.d: a grown-up, like a parent, teacher or counselor, who listens and helps keep you safe
the U.S. Suicide and Crisis Lifeline; call or text 988 any time for free support

look.title: Help Is One Number Away
look.text: The 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline offers free and confidential support, 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, to people in suicidal crisis or emotional distress, by call, text or chat.
look.cite: Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA), 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, 2022 (paraphrase)
look.prompt: Name three ways to reach 988, and name two trusted adults in your own life you could talk to.

check.q: What should you do if a friend says they are thinking about hurting themselves?
choices: Tell a trusted adult right away
check.why: The reading says not to keep it secret but to tell a trusted adult right away.

check.q: How can someone reach the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline?
choices: By calling or texting 988, or chatting online
check.why: 988 can be reached by call, text or chat, any time, for free.

check.q: Which person is an example of a trusted adult?
choices: An older student you just met
Someone who asks you to keep secrets
check.why: A school counselor is a grown-up who listens and helps keep you safe.

lessons.title: Growing Up: Puberty
lessons.mainIdea: Puberty is a normal time of growth and change, and a parent, school nurse or doctor can answer questions about it.
reading: Look at a class photo from fifth grade and another from eighth grade. Many students look very different. That is because of *puberty*, the stage when a child's body gradually grows into an adult body. It is guided by *hormones*, chemical messengers made by glands and carried in the blood.

Puberty often starts sometime between about ages 8 and 14. Everyone's timing is different, and early, middle and later timing are all normal. Common changes include a growth spurt, stronger body odor, and skin changes like pimples. Feelings can also shift more quickly. Daily showers, deodorant, and washing your face help with some of these changes.

Questions about puberty are normal and important. The best people to ask are a parent or guardian, a school nurse or a doctor. They can give correct information that fits you. Your health class may also cover it. Because every body grows on its own schedule, comparing yourself to friends is not a useful measure.

words.d: the stage when a child's body gradually grows and changes into an adult body
a chemical messenger made by a gland and carried in the blood to other parts of the body

look.title: Everyone's Own Schedule
look.text: In one seventh-grade class, some students have already had a big growth spurt, and others have not started yet. Two friends, Leo and Ben, are the same age but now differ in height by six inches. Ben wonders if something is wrong.
look.prompt: Using the reading, what could you tell Ben, and who could he ask with his questions?

check.q: What guides the changes of puberty?
check.why: Hormones, chemical messengers carried in the blood, guide puberty.

check.q: Why is comparing yourself to friends during puberty not useful?
choices: Everyone's body grows on its own schedule
check.why: Early, middle and later timing are all normal, since each body has its own schedule.

check.q: Who are good people to ask about puberty?
choices: A parent, school nurse or doctor
check.why: The reading names a parent or guardian, school nurse or doctor as the best people to ask.

choices: A whole-grain sandwich with vegetables, fruit and milk
review.why: MyPlate includes fruits and vegetables, grains, protein and a calcium-rich food.

review.q: How many hours of sleep do experts recommend for teens?
review.why: The American Academy of Sleep Medicine recommends 8 to 10 hours for teens 13 to 18.

review.q: Why can nicotine affect teens more than adults?
choices: The teen brain is still developing its connections
Nicotine is only sold to teens
review.why: The prefrontal cortex and brain pathways are still developing, and nicotine can affect them.

review.q: Which statement about vaping is accurate?
review.why: Most vapes contain nicotine, and surveys show most teens do not vape.

review.q: What did Dev do that shows refusal skills?
choices: He said no clearly and suggested getting pizza
He took the vape to be polite
review.why: Dev said no clearly and suggested another activity, two refusal steps.

review.q: Which is a healthy coping skill for stress?
choices: Slow breathing and talking with someone you trust
review.why: Slow breathing and talking with a trusted person are coping skills from the chapter.

choices: The Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, free by call or text
The number of hours to sleep
review.why: 988 is the U.S. Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, launched in 2022.

review.why: Not waking up can be an overdose, and the chapter says to call 911 right away.
